decisions.title: When does the agent re-engage to weigh a decision's impact?
decisions.body: Two candidates were named: only when the frontier is empty but the map is not settled (the end of a round), or asynchronously whenever a node enters the pending state, unlocking it when the result lands. A third reading treats the skill's own frontier as the lock: a pending analysis is an unsettled prerequisite, tasks are keyed by their target node over the current upstream state, and at most one task per target is live.

options.text: Per-target asynchronous task the moment a node goes pending; the frontier is the lock; a later upstream answer supersedes the task in flight for that target rather than queuing behind it.
pcr: the human keeps answering everything not downstream; race one closes by construction (one live task per target, always over current upstream state)
one task per pending target, possibly re-run when upstream moves again; the wider-mutation race stays open and is d3/d8's to close
d3's output contract and d5's lock hardness decide the rest

options.text: Only when the frontier is empty and the map is not settled — one reassessment of the whole board, the round end from the grilling skill.
pcr: no races at all; the agent sees every answer of the round together; restructuring is coherent
the human waits at every round end for one long expert turn, and answers a whole frontier on possibly stale structure
makes d6's pre-compute the only source of mid-round speed, and d8 moot

options.text: Both: per-target tasks for one-hop impact during the round, and a whole-board reassessment when the frontier empties.
pcr: mid-round speed and end-of-round coherence
two mechanisms, two seats' worth of cost, and a round-end wait the human has declined
d7's terminal round becomes a special case of the round-end reassessment

decisions.title: What makes a node pending — the mark, or a ruling?
decisions.body: The mark is the map author's prediction at creation; the ruling is a judgment made after the answer. The bake-off showed cheap seats treat the mark as a kill order and the expert treats it as a question, and the expert also touched a node no mark named. So: is an absent mark 'safe' or 'unknown', and is a human-entered note or free-text answer always pending?

options.text: The mark plus any human note or free answer. Absent mark means safe: an unmarked option unlocks its downstream nodes immediately.
pcr: zero wait on every unmarked path; nothing to pre-compute for them
the author's omission is trusted absolutely — a node the ruling would have revised stays open and may be answered on stale structure
d6's pre-compute only has to cover marked options

options.text: Absent mark means unknown: every option is pre-ruled one hop out before the node is offered, and only a pre-ruling of 'unchanged' unlocks the downstream node without a task.
pcr: nothing is trusted that was not judged; the mark becomes a hint to the pre-ruler, not a gate
one judgment per option per decision at map creation and on every refresh — the whole cost of d6
d4's seat choice sets that cost; d6 is forced

options.text: The mark plus notes, as (a), and a background whole-board pre-ruling that upgrades an unmarked option to marked when the pre-ruler disagrees with the author.
pcr: unmarked paths are fast now and corrected later; the author's omissions are caught without blocking
a correction can arrive after the human already answered downstream — a proposal to revisit, which is a race by another name
d8's conflict rule has to cover a pre-ruling correction landing on an answered node

decisions.title: What may an analysis task's result touch?
decisions.body: The second race exists only if a task may mutate outside its target — add a node, revise a neighbour. If a task's result is confined to its own target and anything wider is a proposal for the inbox, conflicting wider proposals become the human's to adjudicate, which the board already does.

options.text: Confined to the target: 'unchanged' unlocks the node as it was; a revise or invalidate of the target is a proposal; anything wider (add-node, other nodes) is a proposal too.
pcr: race two collapses into the inbox; no auto-mutation beyond an unlock; consistent with the board's sole-author rule
the human applies more proposals; a pending node stays pending until they act on its proposal
d8 is a rule about how the inbox shows conflicting proposals, not an agent

options.text: Auto-apply changes to the target (revise/invalidate land and the node unlocks in its new shape); wider changes are proposals.
pcr: fewer clicks; the node the human is about to answer is already correct
an agent rewrites a decision the human may be reading; the constraint on auto-mutation has to be amended
d5's lock hardness matters more — a soft lock over an auto-rewritten node is a footgun

options.text: Auto-apply everything a task concludes, with a conflict-resolution agent when two tasks disagree.
pcr: the board is always the agents' best current picture
a second agent, a merge rule, and the human watching the map change under them — the complexity the impetus names
d8 becomes a design of its own

decisions.title: Which seat weighs impact, in the background and on demand?
decisions.body: Measured on the timed-out turn: cheap seats 7-27s and shallow; the expert 45-61s at every effort and right — at medium already. A human answering the next node takes roughly 10-30s, so a cheap seat rarely makes them wait and an expert usually does, unless the ruling was pre-computed.

options.text: The expert at medium effort for every impact task, pre-computed where d6 allows so the wait is paid before the click.
pcr: the ruling is the one that reads the board; medium loses nothing measured against xhigh
≈45s per task; every pending-with-note node is a real wait
d6's pre-compute is what makes this tolerable; without it the human waits at every marked option

options.text: A cheap seat for in-session tasks, the expert only for nodes pending on a human note or free answer.
pcr: ≤ 20s on most pending nodes
the cheap seats rubber-stamp the mark — the ruling that unlocks a node is the shallow one, and the missing-decision finding never happens mid-session
d7's terminal round becomes where the expert catches what the cheap seat missed

options.text: The expert for pre-computation at map creation and refresh (background, unmeasured by the human); a cheap seat for anything that must run while the human waits.
pcr: judgment where there is time for it, speed where there is not
two seats' rulings on the same board can disagree; the pre-ruling and the live ruling need a precedence rule
d6 must state what a refresh is and how often

decisions.title: The lock is hard — what release does the human have from a pending node?
decisions.body: d1(a) made the frontier the lock: a live task on a target is an unsettled prerequisite, so the node is not offered while the task runs. Answering a pending node in parallel is therefore off the table. What remains is what the human may do about a wait they do not want to sit through.

options.text: No release: the node waits until its task returns; the board names the node and what it is waiting on.
pcr: every answer is made on judged structure, with no override class to record or reason about
the wait is the seat's latency — ≈45s per pending node on the expert without pre-compute
a task that fails or never returns locks the node with no way out

options.text: Transfer: the human may move a pending task to a faster seat, shortening the wait; they still cannot answer until a result lands.
pcr: a long wait becomes a short one on demand, and the human chooses when depth is worth paying for
the shallow ruling is then the one that unlocks the node; the board must show which seat ruled
makes d4's seat choice a default rather than a fixed rule

options.text: Discard: the human may cancel a pending task and answer the node unjudged; the cancellation and the unjudged answer are recorded in history, and the cancelled task's result is dropped rather than landing late.
pcr: the human is never stuck behind an agent, and no late result can land on an answered node — the drop closes that race outright
an answer on unjudged structure is exactly the failure the pending state exists to prevent; history is the only thing that catches it
removes one conflict class from d8: no proposal ever arrives for a node answered under discard

decisions.title: What is pre-computed, and when is it stale?
decisions.body: Pre-ruling every option of every decision is combinatorial deep in the tree; one hop from each settled decision is bounded, and it is where the human clicks next. A pre-ruling is stale when the board moved under it.

options.text: One hop: for every offered decision, each option's impact on its marked (or, under d2(b), all directly connected) nodes is pre-ruled; stale when the pre-ruling's basis seq is older than the last mutation touching any of those nodes; refreshed in the background when stale.
pcr: the happy path costs the human nothing; the set is bounded by the frontier's fan-out
a background expert call per offered option after every mutation — a token cost that scales with the frontier
d1(a)'s per-target task is the same computation run on demand; one mechanism, two triggers

options.text: No pre-compute: only the lock and the on-demand task.
pcr: nothing to keep fresh; simplest possible
every marked option costs a full task wait
makes d4(b)'s cheap seat almost forced

options.text: Whole-map pre-ruling at creation only, never refreshed; anything the session moves falls back to on-demand tasks.
pcr: one up-front cost, paid before the human arrives
the first restructuring makes most of it stale; the map author's plan shape is what is pre-ruled, not the session's
d1(a) carries the rest

decisions.title: Does the board owe the grilling skill's exit criterion — acceptance criteria with IDs and the edge-case taxonomy?
decisions.body: The skill does not end until acceptance criteria are enumerated with stable IDs, each red-test-convertible, each taxonomy row (inverse, boundary, dependency failure, repeated/concurrent, idempotency) resolved or ruled out. The board ends on a prose stop condition. This is separable from the locking question: a stop-the-world terminal round is compatible with async everything before it.

options.text: A terminal round: when the frontier empties, the expert enumerates acceptance criteria and taxonomy rows as decisions on the board, and End is offered only when they are settled or ruled out.
pcr: the board's result carries what the skill's does; the readiness gate downstream has something to read
one long expert turn at the end and a second frontier the human must work
d1(b)/(c)'s round-end reassessment is the same turn

options.text: Keep the prose stop condition; the capture step after End enumerates acceptance criteria from the log, with no further human round.
pcr: no extra wait in the session
criteria nobody argued with; the taxonomy rows are the agent's guess
the session's result is weaker than the skill's, and the readiness gate must tolerate it

options.text: Acceptance criteria accumulate during the session: every settled decision mints its criterion and taxonomy rows as pending proposals, applied as the human goes.
pcr: no terminal wait; criteria are argued as they arise
more inbox traffic per decision; taxonomy rows on early decisions go stale when later ones restructure
d3's output contract must allow a task to propose criteria

decisions.title: When two results disagree — two tasks each proposing a different new node, or a pre-ruling correcting an answered node — what happens?
decisions.body: Race two in its worst form: results that were independent when started but conflict when combined. The rule depends on whether results are proposals or mutations.

options.text: Proposals that target the same node, or both add a node for the same decision, are grouped in the inbox as one conflict; applying one dismisses the rest; nothing is merged by an agent.
pcr: no new agent; the human adjudicates once, with both sides visible
the human does the merge when both proposals are half right
requires d3(a) or (b) — results are proposals

options.text: Last result wins for the same target; earlier results are superseded silently, with history recording what was dropped.
pcr: no conflict surface at all
a correct earlier result can be dropped by a later shallow one; two add-nodes for one decision still collide
only coherent with d1(a)'s one-live-task-per-target rule

options.text: A conflict-resolution turn on the expert merges disagreeing results into one proposal.
pcr: the human sees one coherent proposal
another expert turn, another wait, and a merge whose provenance is hard to show in history
the complexity the impetus warns against; only if d3(c) is taken

decisions.title: What happens when an impact task fails or never returns?
decisions.body: Under d1(a) a live task takes its target off the frontier, so a task that never returns locks that node. Today an unreachable seat and an appender refusal are both terminal with no board-visible trace (9k9.309, 9k9.306), so nothing distinguishes a slow task from a dead one. The constraint that the human is never told to wait without the board naming what they wait on binds here.

options.text: A finite deadline per task: on expiry the node unlocks, marked unjudged, and the expiry is recorded on the decision.
pcr: no node can lock forever; the worst case is the deadline, not the seat's latency
the unlock hands over a node whose impact was never weighed — the unjudged answer of d5(c), reached by inaction rather than choice
this is the 9k9.308 configurable timeout given a board-visible consequence, not a new mechanism

options.text: Failure holds the lock and shows on the board as a named blocker; only a human release clears it.
pcr: no answer is ever made on unjudged structure, and the board says exactly what is stuck and why
coherent only with d5(b) or d5(c) — under d5(a) a dead seat parks the node permanently
needs the board-visible failure trace that 9k9.306 and 9k9.309 say does not exist yet; blocked until it does

options.text: One retry on a faster seat, then the deadline unlock of (a).
pcr: a transient seat failure costs seconds instead of a ruling
the retry's ruling is the shallow one; the board must show the unlock came from the cheaper seat
folds d5(b)'s transfer into the failure path automatically, so d5(b) buys nothing extra

threads.title: d1 — For option C, I'm not sure how that

turns.text: For option C, I'm not sure how that would work because the frontier grows as I answer nodes. The only time I would get to a point where the frontier is locked would be if all the remaining nodes were in a pending or updating state, right?
Option C's round-end reassessment triggers only when the frontier empties — when every currently offered node has been answered — and not when nodes enter a pending state.

Now you need to walk this through. Imagine that we have a board with just two nodes, A and B. B depends on A, so without A being settled, B is locked, and A is the frontier. Once I click a choice on A, as long as that choice does not put B into some form of pending state, the frontier moves to include B, right?

Yes, B enters the frontier the moment A is settled and any downstream task clears. The question this turns on is whether the absence of a pending state means B is immediately answerable or whether it waits for the background task to confirm its upstream basis.

So is it safe to say that "whole board reassessment when the frontier empties" would only happen if any of the node settlements triggered a reassessment of the board that put the last node into pending.  But the trouble with that is that it became pending because there's now an open task against B, which will resolve itself by declaring some change to B, which then opens B up as a frontier node if that change is accepted.

That identifies the exact loop Option C creates: an end-of-round reassessment depends on an empty frontier, but a pending task keeps the frontier open by definition. The question this turns on is whether the round-end trigger should be discarded in favour of per-target tasks alone, or whether empty frontier must be redefined to include pending nodes.

d5.why: A live task is now an unsettled prerequisite, so a pending node is not offered — the soft option contradicts the settled answer, and the live question is what release the human has from the wait.

d3.why: The answer fixes when a task runs and how many are live per target; what a result may touch is untouched, and d1(a)'s own reading leaves the wider-mutation race to d3.

d7.why: Its question survives, but d1(a) removed the round-end reassessment: d7(a) is now a standalone expert turn with a wait of its own, not a reuse of one already there.
